items.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
items.author: Jonathan Wilson
items.content:
There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms

Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

There’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms

F ootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “ spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week , the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules , or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.…

items.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
items.content: <article>Ukraine's president sharply criticised the move, calling it an "investment in war that must be ended, not prolonged".</article>
items.lbText:
US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel into the global market.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Putin later said Russia was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, meanwhile, said any easing of sanctions on Russia played into Moscow's hands and would prolong the war.

Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US, as he has spent months grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which began in February, and its impact on global energy prices.

That conflict has sent the cost of petrol and, in particular diesel, skyrocketing in America in recent months, which has soured his standing with the public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation.

The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.

Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

The BBC understands the Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April 2027 but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Putin said in a statement that he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large.

An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

But Zelensky hit out at it, saying "gifts to Putin will not work for peace" and that Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on social media.

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

According to the International Energy Agency, its diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.

Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.

But on Friday Zelensky defended the strikes, saying there were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".

"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information and the details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return is unclear.

But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US, that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.

What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment on what reimbursement the US is providing Russia in return for the release of diesel.

With the looming US midterm congressional elections - which will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.

Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline, and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.

Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns, and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote

The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference.

The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October.

Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote.

“The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028.

“These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.”

In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election.

Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023.

He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.

Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits.

Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

items.lbText:
Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic

The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review.

The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb).

But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage .

The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing.

The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “ promises kept ” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken , injure or kill people.

But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception.

Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science.

“The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues.

“I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added.

The FDA did not respond to a request for comment.

The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”.

Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts.

Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”.

Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity.

Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical.

“They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.”

The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats.

Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

Perchlorate reduces the thyroid gland’s ability to absorb iodine, which is a raw material needed to produce the hormone T4, an essential component of proper brain development . Very low levels of perchlorate exposure are linked to lower T4 production, and lower IQ scores for children.

Still, six months after it published its data, the FDA reapproved perchlorate for use in super sacks. Advocates say the agency used flawed science and manipulated the data. The FDA wrote that there was no meaningful increase in perchlorate across all the 250 foods it measured. But critics countered that the problem was not in all the food – the problem was in kids’ cereal.

The FDA largely ignored the cereal findings, and mostly does not consider endocrine system harms when developing regulations, said Tom Neltner, a former scientist with the EDF who is now director of the Unleaded Kids non-profit. He helped lead litigation over perchlorate, which was ultimately dismissed.

“They put their blinders on and approved the exemption based on data that never considered the harms posed by endocrine disruptors,” Neltner said.…

items.lbText:
Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying

T he Duchess of Sussex is no ordinary home cook, but when Meghan appeared on Instagram this week at a hob presided over by a special pot filler tap , it spoke to a shift in the everyday kitchen – the rise of “cheffy” kit.

While the pot filler is now most often found in luxury residential kitchens, it was reportedly invented in the early 20th century as a functional fixture for commercial kitchens. It joins a wealth of other restaurant equipment to have infiltrated our homes, from squeezy olive oil bottles to stainless steel mixing bowl sets.

At Sous Chef, a UK-based independent speciality food brand, sales of chef presses are up 26%, while sales of chef’s trays are booming, according to Holly Thomson, the company’s food editor.

For Ella Risbridger, author of The Kitchen Book: Good Food for Every Day : “It’s an amazing thing, the blurring of lines between restaurant and home kitchens.” A byproduct of the increasing visibility we have of professional chefs at work, whether via open kitchens in restaurants or “chefluencers” on social media, the utilitarianism and gadgets of restaurant kitchens are increasingly aspirational. This week, in a home tour with Architectural Digest, Julianne Moore showed off her Ikea industrial shelves.

“People now can see what is happening in professional kitchens,” says Risbridger, “and likely, if they are watching The Bear or a lot of cheffy Instagrams, the algorithm knows that and knows what you might, might, want to buy for yourself.” From the white T-shirt to the Japanese Hasegawa chopping board , people want to channel Carmy and Syd as they make dinner midweek.

Thomson suspects it might have something to do with the economic climate – people are thinking: “‘I’m not going to spend 90 quid on a meal, but I might invest in these products that are going to help me take eating at home a bit more seriously.’” According to James Lawless, a spokesperson at David Mellor, this shift links back to the pandemic, which “reignited interest in home cooking”.

“Professional chefs’ equipment may have specialist functions, but it isn’t special,” says Lawless. “They are first and foremost tools to perform a particular function.”

For Thomson, they are “an extra piece of kit that adds a bit of ease, finesse, or streamlines the process”. Coming from a professional kitchen, where “you don’t have anything that takes up space that isn’t fully useful, used every day and has multiple purposes,” they’d have to be.

Of course, one person’s useful can be another’s waste of space. In the case of the pot filler tap, in an ordinary small kitchen that might be unnecessary, but, according to Helen Parker, the creative director of deVOL Kitchens, it “has become the must-have addition to a larger kitchen”.

Sometimes, you don’t know what you don’t know. As Thomson says of the squeezy olive oil bottle, which, at a few quid, is proof that this isn’t all about expensive equipment: “Precision squirting is just so useful, and once you’ve done it once, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is so much better than glugging oil out of a bottle.’”

For Risbridger, “the trick is that it’s nice to buy something fancy for a hobby – it’s often a shortcut to taking yourself more seriously … you can now access a reasonably cheap version of something professionals use, and that makes you feel more like a professional. Which increases confidence. Which makes the thing you make better, whether or not you could have achieved it without the gadget.”

Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat

V isitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest.

But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best.

As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of the Tobago Hotel and Tourism Association , says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have.

“There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds.

With that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the government agency Eteck , which manages and develops economic zones.

Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas.

Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point.

Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago.

“Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says.

He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry.

Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised.

“The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels.

Michelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist and director at the NGO SpeSeas , says more than 100 people submitted written objections to the Environmental Management Authority (EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments.

After the adjustments, the EMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC , with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow.

Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring.

Cazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”.

Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says.

She adds that the trees provide shade and help protect the beach from coastal erosion, and their removal would harm one of Tobago’s most important turtle nesting sites. “At Back Bay, the shade keeps the sand cool,” she says, making it a choice for hawksbill turtles and leatherback turtles laying their eggs.

Cazabon-Mannette says that sediment runoff from development could also threaten the unique coral reef that makes it a surfer’s paradise. The developer has promised to set up silt fences during construction to control sediment runoff, but “these things fail all the time”, Kenny says.

When questioned about the concerns of environmentalists, John Aboud, chairman of Superior Hotels T&T, replied to the Guardian by forwarding the CEC, without further comment.

While the EMA approval has been issued, final approvals from Tobago’s Town and Country Planning Division and the assembly, its legislative body, remain under review.…

items.lbText:
Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale

U nion officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after the Trump administration unilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints.

“People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth.

TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”.

Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs.

“People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.”

“Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.”

Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturers recommend sitting while operating the machines.

Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations.

Following the policy change, TSA workers were also required to sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union.

“They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones.

He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US.

Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents.

US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy.

“A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.”

AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees, launched a letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”.

Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented.

“Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.”

The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facing possible pay freezes and significant increases to their health insurance premium costs.

Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judge ruling in January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction.

TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year.

The Trump administration has also been expanding privatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airport abandoned its plan to join the program.

TSA did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the policy change and union’s criticisms of the policy and morale pledge. TSA still requires a chair must be available upon request for travelers.

“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News on the policy change, but did not cite why the agency did not negotiate the change with the union.

“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan

Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales.

Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.

When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere.

Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople.

Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16.

“I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape.

In its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer.

When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”.

As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annual cultural festival , held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan.

Evans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim.

The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week.

The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs.

“The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.”

Indeed, online fashion reviews praise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way.

Such premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge.

Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost when the Duchess of Sussex wore a pair during her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders.

Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company.

One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan.

He says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies.

“We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.”

The family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots.

He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.”

Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine.

Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027.…

Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies

The new owner of the Telegraph is preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.

Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant.

A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas.

They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”.

A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far.

It would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale ended three tortuous years for the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.

The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”.

At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth.

Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation.

Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost the Telegraph’s US operation , with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans.

However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles.

Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions.

A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”.

“The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.”

The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m.

However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.

items.lbText:
George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field

The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.

The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.

The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.

“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.

In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.

“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.

Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”

He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation , and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030 .

“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.

“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK .”

Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”

Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.

Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.

In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.

Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”

“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.

“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.

Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”

He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”

Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards .

“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

items.lbText:
With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry

With the Met Office warning that this year’s supersized El Niño could mean a wet and stormy winter lies ahead, it’s never been more important to maintain your home.

Payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% to £244m in 2025 amid the destruction caused by the heavy rain and strong winds that accompanied the likes of Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.

But that is just part of the picture, with total claims for weather damage to homes and possessions hitting £758m last year, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). It says this figure points to “the toll that increasingly severe weather is taking on homes”.

However, experts say regular maintenance can help prevent damage to your property. With that in mind, here are practical steps you can take to make sure your home is best-placed to ride out the storms.

Alex Peters, a cost guide expert at Checkatrade, says : “ The primary line of defence begins at roof level, where high winds will dislodge weak structures and create hazardous flying debris that could damage your home.”

Tiles often become broken or loose, or slip. Ideally you would get up there to have a look, but only do so if you have the proper safety equipment – otherwise, call a professional.

Peters says: “It is important to undertake regular roof and chimney inspections to make sure they’re structurally sound. A standard professional roof inspection averages about £250 per visit to check for loose tiles or mortar decay.”

Most roof repairs cost between £110 and £160 a sq metre, depending on roof type and materials, according to Checkatrade.

A buildup of moss can cause moisture damage to tiles and the wood underneath them, so remove it if you can. The best time is after a dry spell, when you can brush it off with a stiff broom (but don’t attempt this without the proper safety equipment).

Roof “furniture” such as chimneys, skylights and vents is sealed with metal strips called flashing, which should sit flush, with no gaps where water can seep in. If yours does not, you can buy flashing strips, roof sealant and caulk in most DIY stores but, again, this repair job might be better-suited to a professional.

Peters says: “Gutters channel heavy rain safely away from your roofline down to external drains, but if they’re blocked, water can pool and lead to a range of issues.”

These include water seeping into brickwork and causing internal damp, or uncontrolled drainage which erodes the soil around your home’s foundations and, over time, can destabilise them.

Now is a good time to clean them out and make any repairs. The cost depends on the size of your home but sits at about £20-30 an hour for a skilled tradesperson, according to Checkatrade.

Andy Simms, of home service marketplace MyBuilder, says that any trees near your house should be checked now, adding: “Overhanging or unhealthy trees can cause all sorts of property damage, alongside clogging drains.”

Pruning can usually be completed for about £100, but for bigger jobs, a tree surgeon typically costs £240-£400 a day depending on where you live.

Inspect walls for obvious weak spots, including cracked render, staining or places where rainwater collects.

Michael Davie, from specialist home improvement firm PureBuilt, says one of the biggest issues homeowners underestimate is damp caused by small external defects. “A cracked or damaged section of render might not look serious at first, but if water is able to get behind it, the problem can spread quickly,” he says.

“We regularly see cases where what could have been a relatively straightforward repair becomes a much bigger job because the source of the moisture has been left untreated. A repair of about £500 can turn into thousands of pounds once damp has affected plaster, internal finishes or larger areas of the property.”

Repair any cracks or seals around your doors and windows. Peters says: “If there are any gaps or cracks, apply draught excluder tape or caulk to help prevent drafts and water from getting in.”

Window sealant costs about £10 for a 300ml tube, while draught-proofing tape works out at £5-£15 a roll. Another low-cost fix is a door seal – typically a piece of rubber, vinyl or silicone fitted around the frame or on the door edge. You can use basic self-adhesive foam strips or spend more on brush seals and compression strips (and don’t forget letterbox and keyhole covers).

Hiring a professional to weatherstrip drafty openings runs at about £50 a window or £100 for each external door, according to Checkatrade.

Plant pots, garden furniture and trampolines should be stored inside or secured before a storm. Gates and fences are particularly susceptible to wind damage and for this reason most standard buildings insurance policies will not let you claim for the cost of repairing them.

You could reinforce your fence with concrete posts and look at replacing the panels with ones that are 50% wind-permeable (these have gaps that let the wind through without toppling over). For repairs, the price varies depending on the material, but for fence panels it typically costs £45 while fence posts cost about £25. The big cost is labour, and this varies depending on where you live and the amount of work involved, but £950 is a ballpark figure.

Damage caused by frozen and burst pipes can be significant. Household insurers settled roughly 8,000 claims for weather-related pipe damage in 2024, paying out £250m in total, according to the ABI. The average claim was almost £33,000.

Insulating exposed hot water pipes is an easy DIY job. Inexpensive pipe insulation (often called pipe lagging) is available from most DIY stores, and fitting it could also shave about £6 off your annual energy bill, according to the Energy Saving Trust .…

items.lbText:
Competition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in years

National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.

Competition in the savings market has been growing, leading to some of the highest interest rates for years .

However, in the current climate, attractive deals do not always hang around for long, says Rachel Springall at the financial data website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk. If a provider attracts enough savings cash it will pull a product from sale.

NS&I has upped the rates on its “British savings bonds”, which are rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds. They offer a fixed interest rate over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.

The deals are available to new customers and those with existing accounts that are maturing. With the growth version, interest is added each year and paid when the bond matures, while with the income version, interest is paid monthly.

Looking at the growth bonds, the new interest rate on the one-year product is 4.99% (up from 4.82%), while the two-year rate has risen to 5.07% (was 4.81%). The three-year rate has gone up from 4.83% to 5.1%, while the five-year rate has been increased to 5.17% (was 4.85%).

Those are pretty competitive rates, though as Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the advice firm AJ Bell, says, “you can still make more money elsewhere”.

At the time of writing, the top-paying one-year fixed-rate bond was paying 5.12%, while the highest-paying five-year fixed bond was offering 5.37%. But getting the very highest rates sometimes means signing up with less-well-known names. The one-year deal is from Union Bank of India (UK), while the five-year version hails from GB Bank.

If you have a very large sum that you need to stash somewhere – for example, the proceeds of a house sale or an inheritance – these NS&I bonds have one big thing in their favour: you can invest up to £1m per person in each bond issue. The minimum investment is £500.

As NS&I says, “most banks only guarantee your savings up to £120,000,” whereas it is backed by the Treasury and is “the only provider that secures 100% of your savings above this amount”.

Also, it means you are putting your money into the government’s savings bank, and “your savings will be invested back into supporting the UK”.

Money invested in NS&I’s British savings bonds cannot be withdrawn before the end of the fixed term.

That will not suit everyone, and it is a good idea to keep some money in a high-paying easy access account to cover things such as unexpected bills. Earlier this month the digital bank Starling announced that people who sign up for its Easy Saver account will enjoy a table-topping 5% interest rate. This account offers unlimited penalty-free withdrawals, but that rate (made up of a 2.5% variable standard rate, plus a 2.5% fixed interest bonus lasting for six months) only applies to those who open, or have opened, a Starling current account on or after 1 October. The rate applies on balances of up to £25,000.

Starling customers who signed up before then can benefit from a 4% rate when opening a new Easy Saver. That includes a 1.5% fixed interest bonus for six months.

Meanwhile, the savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.

items.lbText:
Exclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship starts

A national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work, the government is to be told.

Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis , will call for a new “national pre-apprenticeship route” to offer young people further education, training and work experience.

Setting out the recommendation from his highly awaited final report – which has been delayed until after this month’s budget – the former Labour cabinet minister warned action was required to address a dramatic plunge in the number of youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.

Against a backdrop of soaring youth unemployment , as few as one in five apprenticeship starts currently go to a 16- to 18-year-old. The number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.

The detail comes as Andy Burnham’s government delays Milburn’s full recommendations until at least November, amid concerns in Downing Street that his report could sit uneasily alongside the 28 October budget.

A former minister in Tony Blair’s cabinet, Milburn has signalled that a shake-up of Britain’s benefits system would form a central plank of his report, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships.

In response, ministers are exploring plans for sweeping welfare changes, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have signalled readiness to stem the government’s rising benefits bill. Other senior Labour figures, including the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, have said there is both a moral case and an economic one to overhaul the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.

However, the government is taking a cautious approach to avoid provoking a repeat of the welfare rebellion which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.

Milburn’s review had been scheduled for launch next week.

Sources close to the review confirmed the delay, although downplayed its significance. One said that Downing Street was working to decide how to present the report alongside several other big reviews, including the Timms review into disability benefits, as well as the budget and the prime minister’s 10-year plan for government.

Burnham has promised to tackle the rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million at the top of his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships .

Currently, as few as 2% of people starting apprenticeships were previously Neet.

Presenting the details of his pre-apprenticeship plan, Milburn said his call for a new programme in England would be targeted at young people who lack the qualifications, confidence, workplace experience or routines needed to secure and sustain a full apprenticeship.

Delivered mainly through further education colleges, it would combine English and maths with technical learning and hands-on experience with an employer. The proposal would be similar to a one-year pre-vocational pathway in Austria that is designed to prepare young people for progression into apprenticeships.

Other countries with much lower Neet rates than the UK have placed much greater emphasis on vocational routes, including the Netherlands and Austria, where more than half of 15- to 19-year olds in upper-secondary education enrol in vocational programmes.

This month, the government announced an expansion in local apprenticeship services, backed by £100m of funding, in a programme delivered by regional mayors, across two years, to double the number of areas matching young people with local businesses.

Milburn said young people had been told for years to go and get an apprenticeship. “But for many young people there is a gap between leaving school and being ready for a full apprenticeship,” he added.

“They may need to improve their English or maths or get more experience of a workplace. And employers understandably want to know that someone is ready to turn up, learn the job and stick at it.

“I want a new national pre-apprenticeship route. A course done through colleges, combining English and maths, technical training and proper experience with an employer. Geared towards one thing: getting a young person into work.”

items.lbText:
Waves of protests expose debt crisis faced by French government, but political wrangling is stalling an escape plan. Is there a way out?

E ight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace.

As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests , but this time the financial markets are unhappy too.

Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets . But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole.

France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025 , while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively.

In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how.

One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef , France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy. In a warning to all politicians, 66% said their business would become vulnerable or even go bankrupt if economic policy remained deadlocked for the next five years.

A rescue operation could be mounted by the European Central Bank (ECB), but France would demand unconditional support when the ECB’s rules say bailouts must come with strict conditions.

Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at Insead, the European business school, says the political and economic situation has pushed France to the edge of a financial collapse. “I am very worried about the economic situation because growth is low and it is difficult to see how the dynamics change. Then you have the debt numbers, which are bad, and the financial markets are thinking the government is not in control.

“If I look at the political situation, I am panicking. That’s because too many political parties are saying let France burn. They want a crisis, believing it will improve their share of the vote.”

There is much about the economic situation in France that mirrors what has happened in the UK and the US. A huge spending splurge during the Covid pandemic was followed by another round of subsidies to offset the worst side-effects from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Investors have become wary of lending to all three countries, but the rise in interest rates is strongest in France.

Last week, the yield, or interest rate, on ⁠10-year French bonds hit the highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. Yields go up when bond prices go down.

Japanese investors, typically strong supporters of France as a haven for their savings, have been instrumental in the panic after they found better returns on home turf, heaping further pain on the French treasury.

According to many metrics, it is difficult to see why France should be so badly affected. The French economy has many things going for it, from relatively low electricity prices to better than average infrastructure.

The schools that are the focus of recent protests are better funded than the OECD average.

On the debit side of the ledger, Macron’s plan to raise the pension age from 62 to 64, saving tens of billions of euros from an almost entirely socialised retirement system, stalled at 62 and nine months after parliament was deadlocked after the 2024 snap election . This might have mattered less if the economy was growing, but Macron’s much-vaunted economic revival remains stuck in first gear.

Laurent Warlouzet, a professor of history at the Sorbonne, says it is understandable that international investors are confused about France when Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in presidential elections next year, says she will roll back the retirement age to 62 and at the same time introduce a “debt brake” via a referendum, restricting further borrowing.

He said: “The far right used to be a spendthrift populist force, especially under Le Pen’s leadership, broadening the appeal of National Rally voters in the country’s rust belts. In 2016–17, she still wanted France to leave the eurozone, which she regarded as a straitjacket.”

Warlouzet, the author of Liberty, Solidarity and Community: capitalism and European integration, 1945 to the present, added: “Nowadays, Le Pen has become an improbable fiscal hawk. How can she reconcile this with her voters’ demands for more nurses, teachers, police officers and judges?”

Erik Britton, the director of Fathom Consulting, an international advisory firm, says the prospect of a runoff between Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the leftwing La France Insoumise (LFI), and Le Pen next April has spooked investors more than the failure to bring down the annual deficit.

“What has changed is the likely runoff. In the second round, it now looks likely that Le Pen will contest the presidential election against Mélenchon from the far left. Le Pen’s election might mean a 20% risk of Frexit : Mélenchon’s election, though less likely on current polling, would have a much higher risk of Frexit.”

Britton says the collapse of the centre ground would have implications far beyond its borders. “Where France goes, the euro area as a whole tends to follow. If it led to another test of the euro, all the considerations about debt and debt mutualisation would resurface, and bond yields would pop right across the euro area (perhaps with the exception of Germany) and beyond.”…

items.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
items.content: <article>The stalwart of Britain's High Street has been sold to a Canadian billionaire family. What will that mean for you?</article>
items.lbText:
If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.

The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.

But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.

Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how the easy stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.

Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.

Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."

The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.

Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.

She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.

Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".

"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."

Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".

"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."

The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.

The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.

It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.

Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.

While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.

"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.

Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.

But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.

There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.

For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana
